new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule is stated for Gowro anywhere. Baart only suspects (with a question mark) that Gowro is tonal and tentatively groups it with the 'Shina-type' systems (lexically placed stress on one mora carrying a high tone), by analogy with its neighbours Indus Kohistani and Shina. The only first-hand data are the stress-marked field transcriptions in Hallberg's 1992 survey wordlist (column GAB), where the mark falls on different syllables in different words (initial 'nothu0, 'bVli; final su'rVt, hàlà'li), i.e. lexically variable placement, but the survey explicitly disclaims phonological analysis.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the author explicitly flags Gowro's tonal status as uncertain (question mark) and the classification as tentative.
new_statements.domain_note: Survey-level typological table with no Gowro data; 'Shina-type' is Baart's label for languages where stress is lexically assigned to one mora and realised as a high tone on that mora (Indus Kohistani, Shina, Burushaski, Palula are the certain members). Nothing is said about word vs phrase domain or citation forms for Gowro.
new_statements.identity_note: Gowro = Gabaro = the Gabar Khel clan language of Mahrin village (Kolai area, east bank of the Indus, District Kohistan), glottocode gowr1239, ISO gwf; Hallberg 1992 warns it must not be confused with Gawri (= Kalami/Gawri, gawr1245) of Swat. Zoller's 2005 Indus Kohistani dictionary treats 'Gabār' as a local variety of Indus Kohistani (indu1241) and Bashir equates it with Gowro; Hallberg's 61-63% lexical similarity between Gowro and Indus Kohistani and Jettmar's informants' denial of separateness show the language/dialect status is unsettled. Baart 2003 and Hallberg 1992 both refer to the Mahrin Gabar Khel variety.
